idiom_name: hand-written <table>_gateway functions over sqlite3_prepare_v2 or libpq PQexecParams
implementation_notes: C has no database layer in the standard library, so the gateway is a set of per-table functions plus a plain struct for the row - the record - over a driver such as the SQLite C API or libpq. Both drivers support parameterized execution (sqlite3_prepare_v2 with sqlite3_bind_*/sqlite3_step, or PQprepare/PQexecParams), which replaces string-built SQL and is the only safe way to pass values; the classic table-object structure survives as a naming convention (users_insert, users_find_by_id) and as one prepared-statement cache per connection. Free functions over the handle remain the right form when only a handful of statements exist; a struct of function pointers or an opaque users_gateway_t is justified when several implementations must be interchangeable.
pitfalls: Leaking statement handles: sqlite3_finalize (or PQclear for each PGresult) must run on every path including errors - an unfinalized statement keeps memory and locks pinned until the connection closes.
Building SQL with sprintf instead of bind parameters is the classic C gateway injection hole, because the driver executes whatever string it is handed.
NULL and length discipline: PQgetisnull/PQgetlength and sqlite3_column_bytes must be consulted before reading a value, or NULL and empty string become indistinguishable.
sqlite3_prepare_v3/finalize are not thread-safe on a shared connection in the default threading mode; give each thread its own connection or serialize access.
